title: Symphony No. 3 in D minor
hook: A whole summer in six movements, from sleeping rock to flowers, animals, angels and love.

painting.title: Spring in the Alps
painting.collection: J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
painting.pairingNote: Painted the year after Mahler finished the symphony, it is a hymn to nature waking after winter, with mountains, meadows, animals and people in one picture, which is the Third’s own plan.

facts: Composed mainly in the summers of 1895 and 1896 at Steinbach, on the shore of Lake Attersee in Upper Austria, where Mahler had a small composing hut. He conducted the first complete performance in Krefeld on 9 June 1902.
The longest symphony in the standard repertoire. The first movement alone lasts over half an hour.

Mahler gave each movement a private title, then withdrew them before publication: “Pan awakes, summer marches in”, “What the flowers in the meadow tell me”, “What the animals in the forest tell me”, “What man tells me”, “What the angels tell me” and “What love tells me”.
Two singing movements: a mezzo-soprano sings words by Nietzsche (IV), then women’s and boys’ voices sing a folk poem about angels (V). The last three movements run on without a break.
bigPicture.inOneLine: nature wakes and summer marches in (I), flowers (II), animals (III), the human voice at midnight (IV), angels (V), love (VI).

movements.heading: Kräftig. Entschieden.
movements.title: Kräftig. Entschieden. (Strong. Decisive.)
movements.summary: Part One of the symphony, and a world in itself. Dark, motionless nature slowly stirs, and summer arrives as a noisy, cheerful march that sweeps everything along.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call
mainIdeas.description: eight horns in [[unison|unison]], a bold striding tune.

mainIdeas.name: The sleeping earth
mainIdeas.description: low brass, muffled drums, long silences.

mainIdeas.name: The march of summer
mainIdeas.description: light, chirping woodwinds that grow into a full military band.

stops.hear: Eight horns in unison, loud and proud
stops.happening: The opening call. Its shape recalls the big tune in the finale of Brahms’s First Symphony

stops.hear: A thud of bass drum, then low, groaning brass and long pauses
A trombone solo, slow and declamatory, like a speech
stops.happening: The first of several long trombone solos

stops.hear: Shrill woodwind trills and distant fanfares
The heavy, dark music returns, with the trombone again
Piccolos and clarinets start a light march; it slowly gathers players
The march breaks up, regroups and changes key; a solo violin sings
The march at full force: snare drums, cymbals, blaring brass
Snare drums alone, then the eight horns again
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] begins with the opening call

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Brass fanfares over pounding timpani
stops.happening: A blazing finish in F major

notice: Mahler wrote “there follows a long pause” at the end of this movement in his manuscript. The symphony’s second part starts here.

movements.heading: Tempo di Menuetto
movements.title: Tempo di Menuetto
movements.summary: “What the flowers in the meadow tell me.” After the giant first movement, a delicate [[minuet|minuet]], light and a little old-fashioned. Twice a breeze turns into a gust.

stops.hear: A solo oboe with a graceful tune over plucked strings
Quicker, rustling music in flutes and violins
stops.happening: The first episode, like wind in the grass

stops.hear: The oboe’s tune returns
Faster and stormier, with sharp accents
The minuet once more, gentler than ever

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: A soft pluck of harp and glockenspiel

movements.heading: Comodo. Scherzando. Ohne Hast.
movements.title: Comodo. Scherzando. Ohne Hast.
movements.summary: “What the animals in the forest tell me.” A busy, comic [[scherzo|scherzo]] built on an early Mahler song. Twice it stops for a [[posthorn|posthorn]], playing from far away, like a coach passing through the forest.

stops.hear: Clarinets and piccolo chatter over plucked strings
stops.happening: The animals’ scherzo, from Mahler’s song “Ablösung im Sommer”

stops.hear: Lighter, bouncing music in a skipping rhythm
Everything stops. A [[posthorn|posthorn]] plays a long, nostalgic melody from a distance
A sudden trumpet signal cuts in
stops.happening: An Austrian military call breaks the spell

stops.hear: The chatter starts up again
The posthorn again, even slower, with soft horns

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A sudden blast from the full orchestra

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: A quick, abrupt close

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The posthorn solos are played by John Ware.

movements.heading: Sehr langsam. Misterioso.
movements.title: Sehr langsam. Misterioso.
movements.summary: “What man tells me.” Midnight. A mezzo-soprano sings the “Midnight Song” from Nietzsche’s *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*: the world is deep, its pain is deep, but joy is deeper still and wants eternity.

stops.hear: Low strings rocking between two notes, very softly
The voice enters, low and slow: “O Mensch! Gib acht!” (O man, take heed!)
An oboe slides upwards
stops.happening: A night bird. Mahler asks for a [[glissando|glissando]]

stops.hear: A solo violin and horns warm the music a little
stops.happening: The poem turns from pain to joy

stops.hear: The voice sings its last, long-held line
stops.happening: Joy “wants eternity”: the poem’s final words

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: A soft held chord
stops.happening: The angels’ song follows without a pause

movements.heading: Lustig im Tempo und keck im Ausdruck
movements.title: Lustig im Tempo und keck im Ausdruck
movements.summary: “What the angels tell me.” Boys’ voices imitate church bells while women sing a folk poem from *Des Knaben Wunderhorn* about three angels. The mezzo-soprano sings the part of a sinner who weeps and is promised heaven.

stops.hear: Boys singing “Bimm bamm” like bells, with real bells and glockenspiel
Women’s voices sing a bright, simple tune
The mezzo-soprano enters, troubled
stops.happening: The sinner’s lament: the Ten Commandments have been broken

stops.hear: The music darkens for a moment; a gong sounds
The bells and the bright tune return

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: The bells fade one by one
stops.happening: The final movement begins at once

movements.heading: Langsam. Ruhevoll. Empfunden.
movements.title: Langsam. Ruhevoll. Empfunden.
movements.summary: “What love tells me.” A long, slow hymn for orchestra alone, no voices. It begins in near-silence and climbs, with setbacks, to a radiant end in D major.

stops.hear: Strings alone, very softly, a broad melody that rises step by step
The music grows restless and darker, in the minor
The hymn returns, with woodwinds joining
A long build-up, heavier and heavier
stops.happening: The second contrast, building to a crisis

stops.hear: A harsh, crushing climax, then near silence
A flute and piccolo alone, high above quivering strings, then a quiet brass [[chorale|chorale]]
The hymn begins its final ascent
Trumpets and trombones take the theme, fortissimo

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: Repeated D major chords, with solemn strokes on the timpani

notice: The opening melody of this movement is only a few notes long, but it is never quite the same twice. Try to follow it all the way through.

threads.title: A ladder of being
threads.body: Mahler’s plan climbs from rock and flowers to animals, people, angels and love.

threads.title: Distance
threads.body: Offstage snare drums in the first movement and the posthorn in the third bring sounds from far away.

threads.title: From D minor to D major
threads.body: The symphony opens in D minor and ends in D major, but the long road between them runs through F major and many other keys.
